text: In the high-end fragrance and flavor industry, bergamot (Citrus bergamia) essential oil from Calabria, Italy, is highly sought after.

The unique aroma profile of bergamot (Citrus bergamia) essential oil from Calabria, Italy, primarily composed of linalool and linalyl acetate, makes bergamot essential oil a key component in classic perfume formulations such as eau de cologne.
Furthermore, bergamot (Citrus bergamia) essential oil from Calabria, Italy, has demonstrated potential anxiolytic properties in clinical aromatherapy research.
Essential oil obtained from fingered citron (Citrus medica L. var. sarcodactylis) using cold-pressed supercritical extraction technology has a high content of d-limonene and trace furanocoumarins.

The high content of d-limonene and trace furanocoumarins in the essential oil from fingered citron (Citrus medica L. var. sarcodactylis) imparts a fresh, crisp aroma, making it an important fixative in high-end home fragrances.

In crop protection, essential oil derived from sweet orange (Citrus sinensis) is developed as a highly effective natural insecticide due to the strong dissolving effect of its main component d-limonene on insect cuticles.
Guangdong Xinhui Chenpi, derived from Citrus reticulata 'Chachi', exemplifies the medicinal and culinary use of citrus peel.
Meanwhile, low-salt preserved Chenpi processed from the peel of Citrus reticulata 'Chachi' and other citrus varieties is a popular leisure health snack.
The volatile oils and flavonoids in Xinhui Chenpi (Citrus reticulata 'Chachi') effectively neutralize the gaminess of duck meat.

In food colloid science, high-ester pectin extracted from the peel—especially the albedo—of sweet orange (Citrus sinensis) and other citrus fruits is widely used as an effective gelling agent in low-sugar, high-acidity food systems like jams and jellies.
In the pharmaceutical field, citrus pectin is often used as a matrix material for drug delivery systems due to its good biocompatibility and modifiability.

Hesperidin, sourced primarily from sweet orange (Citrus sinensis), is commonly used as a raw material in health products due to its activities of enhancing capillary toughness, antioxidation, and anti-inflammation.
Nobiletin, primarily derived from citrus peels such as those of Citrus reticulata, is a polymethoxyflavone that attracts significant attention in the screening of anticancer drug lead compounds.

Based on the promoting effect of naringin—abundantly obtained from pomelo (Citrus grandis)—on osteoblast differentiation, researchers are exploring its incorporation as a functional component into bone tissue engineering scaffold materials.
Pomelo sacs from Citrus maxima and orange sacs from Citrus sinensis are produced via modern food processing technologies such as enzymatic softening and aseptic filling.
In molecular gastronomy, reverse spherification using sodium alginate and calcium chloride can encapsulate Satsuma mandarin (Citrus unshiu) juice into "artificial sacs" with a thin film structure.
Pomace after juicing—such as from sweet orange (Citrus sinensis)—can be dried and ground to produce citrus fiber.
As a functional food ingredient, citrus fiber significantly improves the water-holding capacity and texture of baked goods like high-fiber bread.
Citric acid, naturally sourced mainly from lemon (Citrus limon), is one of the world's highest produced and consumed organic acids.
Citric acid’s ability to chelate metal ions also makes it an effective natural preservative aid.
By chelating calcium ions in blood, citrates ensure the safe storage of blood in blood banks.
Citrus seed oil can be obtained from seeds—such as those from grapefruit (Citrus paradisi)—via cold pressing or solvent extraction.
Citrus seed oil is often used as a moisturizing base oil or active ingredient carrier in natural cosmetic formulations.

Comparative studies show significant differences in fatty acid composition—such as the oleic acid to linoleic acid ratio—and tocopherol homologue distribution among citrus seed oils from different varieties, including Citrus reticulata and Citrus limon.
Naringin, extracted from the peels of grapefruit (Citrus paradisi) and other citrus fruits, is a key precursor for synthesizing the new high-intensity sweetener neohesperidin dihydrochalcone.
Synephrine, extracted from the immature fruit of Citrus aurantium (used in Traditional Chinese Medicine as "Zhi Shi") or its peel, is often used in weight management dietary supplements.
Citrus reticulata ‘Chachi’ has been cultivated in Xinhui County of Guangdong Province, which is known as the core region for its production.
Citrus reticulata ‘Chachi’ is also popularly known as ‘Guangchenpi’ (GCRP).
The colony was maintained on CLas-infected ‘Valencia’ sweet orange (Citrus sinensis).

The purpose of this study was to evaluate salicylic acid (SA) and phenylacetic acid (PAA) applied individually by soil drench to young trees of three citrus species: Citrus sinensis (sweet orange), Citrus reticulata (mandarin), and Citrus aurantifolia (Mexican lime).
These citrus species were growing on rootstocks of Citrus volkameriana and Citrus aurantium.
This analysis focused on the self-incompatible ‘Comune’ clementine and its self-compatible natural mutant ‘Monreal’.
The most economically and industrially important representatives of the genus Citrus are oranges (Citrus × aurantium var. sinensis L.).
Lemons (Citrus × limon var. limon (L.) Burm. f.) are also among the most important.
Limes (Citrus × aurantifolia var. aurantifolia) hold significant economic and industrial value.
Grapefruits (Citrus × paradisi) are likewise major representatives of the genus Citrus.
Shiranuhi (also known as Dekopon) originates from the hybridization of ‘Kiyomi’ and ‘Ponkan’.
Shiranuhi is an internationally renowned premium mandarin.
Shiranuhi is celebrated for its explosively sweet flavor and firm texture.
The parentage of Kiyomi is ‘Miyagawa Wase’ Satsuma mandarin crossed with ‘Trovita’ sweet orange.
Kiyomi is a seminal Japanese hybrid that combines the sweetness and seedlessness of Satsuma mandarin with the rich flavor of sweet orange.
Kiyomi has become an extremely important parent in modern citrus breeding.

‘Ehime 38’ (Citrus reticulata), referred to as ‘WT’, and its bud mutant, referred to as ‘MT’, were grafted onto different branches of the same rootstock ‘red tangerine’ (Citrus reticulata).
The dataset included grapefruit (Citrus × paradisi), which belongs to commonly cultivated citrus species and cultivars.
It also included mandarins (Citrus reticulata and Citrus × clementina), which belong to commonly cultivated citrus species and cultivars.
Lemon (Citrus × limon) was included as a commonly cultivated citrus species and cultivar.
Oranges (Citrus × sinensis) were also included as commonly cultivated citrus species and cultivars.

Ethyl 2-methylbutyrate (OAV = 378,624.45), ethyl butyrate (OAV = 44,085.94), and ethyl hexanoate (OAV = 37,730.80) were among the key odorants contributing to the characteristic aroma of HG citrus juice.
Additional important odorants included hexanal (OAV = 4,329.82), (+)-carvone (OAV = 2,751.29), linalool (OAV = 1,939.70), and nonanal (OAV = 1,810.95).

Further contributors were hexyl acetate (OAV = 1,076.69), α-terpineol (OAV = 818.27), β-myrcene (OAV = 740.31), α-ionone (OAV = 548.88), 3-methylbutanol (OAV = 414.96), α-pinene (OAV = 403.61), ethyl 3-hydroxyhexanoate (OAV = 344.85), and d-limonene (OAV = 335.99).
Among these monoterpenes, d-limonene is a major component, accounting for 60% to 95% of the total volatile content.
d-Limonene has a pleasant lemon-like scent and is widely used as an aroma additive in perfumes, cosmetics, and foods.
Pompia essential oils are primarily extracted from the peel and leaves of the fruit.

Essential oils derived from the peel contain a high concentration of the monoterpene limonene (82%), along with much lower levels of myrcene (1.8%), geranial (1.7%), geraniol (1.5%), and neral (1.4%).
In the rind extract, significant amounts of flavanones have been identified, including neoeriocitrin (46.53 µg/mg), neohesperidin (44.57 µg/mg), and naringin (23.77 µg/mg).
The same rind extract also contains gallic acid (128.3 µg/mg) and quinic acid (219.67 µg/mg).
D-Limonene, a monoterpene hydrocarbon, is the primary constituent of citrus essential oils and imparts the characteristic aroma of citrus peels.
Linalool is a monoterpene alcohol that imparts delicate floral and lavender-like aroma notes.
Due to its low odor threshold value (OTV; approximately 6 μg/L), linalool is recognized as a key aroma-active compound in sweet orange juice.
Similarly, α-terpineol is another monoterpene alcohol that contributes clove-like and woody nuances to citrus aroma.
However, α-terpineol has a higher OTV (approximately 330 μg/L), which limits its sensory impact relative to linalool.

Decanal is an aldehyde characterized by an intense citrus peel and waxy odor.It has an extremely low odor threshold value (OTV; approximately 0.1 μg/L), making it a major contributor to the characteristic aroma of sweet orange.
Octanal is another important aldehyde that imparts a fresh, fruity scent.  With an OTV of about 0.7 μg/L, octanal also plays a significant role in citrus aroma perception.
Among ketones, nootkatone is particularly notable for providing the distinctive grapefruit aroma. It has an OTV of approximately 1 μg/L, contributing strongly even at low concentrations.

Citronellal is a monoterpene aldehyde that exhibits a pronounced lemongrass-like scent. Its OTV is about 25 μg/L, which is higher than that of decanal or octanal but still within the range of sensory relevance.
Other relevant volatile compounds include γ-terpinene and 1,8-cineole.
γ-Terpinene contributes herbaceous aroma notes, while 1,8-cineole—an oxygenated monoterpene (oxide)—imparts a cool, camphoraceous character.
Regarding taste perception, sourness in citrus juice is primarily attributed to organic acids.
Citric acid is the predominant acidic component, with a taste threshold of approximately 700 mg/L.
Bitterness is a notable sensory attribute in citrus fruits, especially in certain varieties such as grapefruit.
Among flavonoid glycosides, naringin is identified as the primary bitter compound in grapefruit.It has a taste threshold of approximately 20 mg/L, above which its bitterness becomes perceptible.
Neohesperidin is another bitter flavonoid glycoside, but it exhibits a lower taste threshold of about 5 mg/L, making it more potent on a concentration basis.
In addition, the triterpenoid limonin contributes to a lingering bitter aftertaste.
Limonin has a relatively low taste threshold of around 1 mg/L and is associated with delayed or late-onset bitterness in citrus juices.
Sweetness in citrus juices is primarily provided by soluble sugars, particularly sucrose.
However, sugars such as sucrose have high taste thresholds, meaning relatively large concentrations are needed to elicit a sweet sensation.
For example, glutamic acid—present in citrus juices—has a taste threshold of approximately 150 mg/L and could potentially enhance mouthfeel thickness or contribute to umami perception.

Located in northeastern Guangdong Province (23°23′–24°56′ N, 115°18′–116°56′ E), Meizhou City covers a total area of approximately 15,876.06 km² and features terrain that slopes from higher elevations in the north to lower in the south.
Meizhou City is predominantly hilly and mountainous, comprising 56.6% hills and 24.3% mountains, while plains account for only 13.7% of its land area.

Meizhou City has a subtropical monsoon climate—transitional between southern and central subtropical zones—with a mean annual temperature of 22.1°C, annual precipitation of about 2,139.8 mm, and approximately 1,783 hours of sunshine per year, featuring long, hot summers, short winters, and abundant sunlight.

Kunming City lies on the central Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau between 24°23′ N and 26°33′ N, characterized by a plateau basin topography with an average elevation of about 1,890 meters and relatively gentle terrain.
Kunming City has a unique low-latitude plateau mountain monsoon climate. Its mean annual temperature is about 15°C. Annual precipitation in the city ranges from 900 to 1,200 millimeters.
Known for its “spring-like” weather year-round, Kunming City offers a pleasant climate.Primarily composed of acidic red and yellow earths, its soils provide an ideal foundation for agriculture.
Turpan City is situated in an intermountain basin in the eastern Tien Shan Mountains, at approximately 42°15′ N to 43°35′ N latitude.
Characterized by a typical intermountain depression basin topography, Turpan City is home to Ayding Lake, whose surface lies 154 meters below sea level—the lowest point in China.
Turpan City has an extremely arid continental warm-temperate desert climate, with a mean annual temperature of about 13.9°C.
Turpan City regularly experiences summer extreme temperatures exceeding 49°C.
With only about 16.4 mm of annual precipitation, Turpan City experiences extremely high evaporation rates.
Chongqing Municipality is located in the southeastern part of the Sichuan Basin, spanning approximately 28°10′ N to 32°13′ N latitude.
Shaped by the convergence of the Yangtze and Jialing Rivers, Chongqing Municipality is dominated by hilly and mountainous terrain.
Owing to its river-influenced topography, a distinctive “mountain city” landscape emerges in Chongqing Municipality.
Chongqing Municipality falls under a humid subtropical monsoon climate, with a mean annual temperature ranging from 16°C to 18°C.
Receiving abundant annual precipitation of approximately 1,000–1,350 mm, Chongqing Municipality is notably wet.
Due to its basin topography and frequent overcast or rainy conditions, annual sunshine duration remains relatively low—only 1,000 to 1,200 hours—in Chongqing Municipality.
Chongqing Municipality experiences numerous foggy days throughout the year.
Situated in southeastern China at approximately 30°15′ N latitude, Hangzhou City lies at the junction of the northern Zhejiang plains and hilly regions.
Sloping from higher elevations in the west to lower in the east, Hangzhou City’s terrain combines western hills and mountains with an eastern alluvial plain that belongs to the Yangtze River Delta.
Hangzhou City has a typical northern subtropical monsoon climate with distinct seasons and concurrent rainfall and heat.
Hangzhou City maintains a mean annual temperature of approximately 16.5°C.
With a moderate annual sunshine duration of about 1,800 hours, Hangzhou City enjoys ample daylight.
Receiving annual precipitation between 1,150 mm and 1,450 mm, Hangzhou City experiences a relatively wet climate.
Hangzhou City is primarily covered by red soil and paddy soil.
RICH is a full, heavy mouthfeel and flavor found in slow-cooked meats or cream sauces like alfredo, and is classified under Fattiness.
FATTY describes a smooth, glossy, full-bodied texture in the mouth—distinct from low-fat alternatives—and falls within the Fattiness category.
GREASY refers to the oily residue from cooking that oozes out when biting into fried foods (e.g., funnel cake), a sensation grouped with Fattiness.
SWEET is one of the five basic tastes, signaling the presence of sugars and energy.
FRUITY denotes pronounced, sweet fruit-like notes (e.g., fresh raspberry) and is typically associated with the Sweet taste profile.
HONEYED conveys a natural, full-bodied sweetness with complex background notes (floral, citrus, earthy)—a descriptor categorized under Sweet.
BITTERSWEET blends mild sweetness with depth or tartness, as in unsweetened dark chocolate, and is considered a Sweet-related flavor attribute.
SOUR is a mouth-puckering sensation driven by acids in lemons, yogurt, or sourdough.
CITRUSY describes bright, forward acidity from citrus fruits that stimulates salivation—a flavor falling within the Sour spectrum.
TANGY evokes a tart-sweet, tingly sensation on the palate (e.g., key lime pie) and is classified under Sour.
ZESTY conveys a vivid, invigorating tang from vinegar or citrus, as in pickles—a sensory attribute aligned with Sour.
BITTER is a basic taste that signals potential toxins, causing a dry, pinched mouthfeel (e.g., coffee, cocoa).
SHARP denotes a harsh, biting quality in aged cheeses or over-fermented foods, and is categorized as a Bitter-associated descriptor.
ACRID describes an unpleasantly harsh taste or smell from burned or over-smoked items—a sensation falling within the Bitter domain.
UMAMI is the savory “delicious taste” generated by amino acids during cooking, aging, or fermentation.
FULL-BODIED describes a rich, lingering flavor that fully coats the mouth (e.g., bold red wine), and contributes to the perception of Umami.
NUTTY describes a flavor and aroma reminiscent of nuts—intensified when fats are toasted, as in a dark roux or raw almonds—and is classified under Umami.
SAVORY refers to deeply flavorful, cooked or fermented foods such as cured meats, soy sauce, Parmesan, and mushrooms, and is typically associated with the Umami taste profile.
SALTY is one of the five basic tastes, enhancing overall flavor when balanced but overwhelming the palate in excess.
BRINY denotes a strong, sea-like saltiness found in olives, capers, or pickles, and falls within the Salty category.
BLAND describes underseasoned food lacking flavor intensity—such as plain steamed rice—and is considered a deficit state within the Salty dimension (i.e., absence of salt-driven taste).
PIQUANT conveys a pleasantly sharp, assertive flavor—exemplified by mustard or aged Parmesan—that is categorized as a Salty-associated descriptor due to its saline edge and role in flavor balance.

Lime exhibits a fresh and sour aroma primarily shaped by limonene and citral, with spicy notes from eugenol, floral orange blossom nuances from linalool, and dry, woody, resinous accents contributed by α-terpineol.

Grapefruit displays a clean, slightly bitter herbal character driven by terpenes such as nootkatone and ocimene, complemented by the sweet woody depth of nootkatone and a juicy, spicy sensation from thiols like 1-p-menthen-8-thiol.

Bergamot delivers a sweet, floral lavender-like aroma with citrus freshness, resulting from the interplay of linalyl acetate and limonene, while trace amounts of methyl jasmonate and ionone lactones impart a characteristic smoky undertone.

Blood orange is distinguished by a sweet-and-sour berry-like note from raspberry ketone and β-damascenone, in addition to foundational terpenes like limonene and myrcene; trace aldehydes (nonanal and decanal) further enrich its fruity, waxy character.

Kumquat opens with a sharp pine-and-pepper note from α-pinene and γ-terpinene, develops a dual profile of green peel and fresh florals via neral and citronellal, and finishes with earthy, woody base notes from longifolene and caryophyllene.

Trifoliate Orange (Zhishi) is characterized by α-terpineol and 4-terpineol, which confer a strong resinous and camphoraceous aroma, while phenolic compounds such as eugenol add spicy notes and a faint mint-like coolness.

Mandarin derives its characteristic “orange fragrance” primarily from γ-terpinene: below 44.56 μg/g, it yields a pleasant citrus scent, but excess levels produce a “stinky orange” odor; this profile is complemented by the background citrus note of d-limonene and the soft floral nuance of linalool.

Lime presents a sharp lemon-like freshness dominated by limonene and citronellal, with herbal and woody undertones from γ-terpinene and α-terpineol, as well as warm spicy notes contributed by trace sesquiterpenes such as caryophyllene.

Ichang Papeda features a fresh, pine-like top note from pinene and sabinene, a distinctive oily-waxy fruit character from long-chain esters like methyl tridecanedioate, and a bittersweet, herbal-like scent enriched by coumarins such as umbelliferone and auraptene in the peel.

Australian Finger Lime delivers an intense lemon-like aroma due to high citral content (a mixture of neral and geranial), a spicy-herbal character from thymol and its derivatives, and a caviar-like aromatic burst potentially enhanced by trace thiols such as 1-p-menthen-8-thiol in the pulp.

Canton Lemon exhibits lavender-like floral and rose-like sweet notes from linalyl acetate and geraniol, a subtle peachy-creamy nuance from trace γ-decalactone, and a dry, resinous quality imparted by monoterpene alcohols (e.g., α-terpineol) and linalool oxides in the peel.

Gannan navel orange (Citrus sinensis (L.) Osbeck) contains linalool (OAV ≥ 1) as a key aroma compound, contributing a typical floral and lavender-like scent that significantly shapes the fruit’s overall fragrance profile.

“Chu orange” (Citrus sinensis ‘Chu orange’) features myrcene (OAV ≥ 1) as a characteristic aroma component, which imparts a pleasant balsamic-earthy note and collaborates with limonene to create a fresh overall aroma impression.

Grapefruit (Citrus paradisi) cultivars Jiwei and Fenghongtangmuxun accumulate phenolic acids predominantly in juice vesicles, with gallic acid at 343.7 μg/g dry weight and chlorogenic acid at 110.23 μg/g dry weight.
Navel orange (Citrus sinensis Osbeck) contains hesperidin as the predominant flavonoid in both pulp and peel.
Navel orange (Citrus sinensis Osbeck) flavedo is rich in polymethoxyflavones (PMFs), particularly sinensetin and nobiletin, as revealed by HPLC-Q-TOF/MS analysis.
Pummelo (Citrus grandis) and grapefruit (Citrus paradisi) juices feature naringin as the most abundant bitter compound, with its concentration strongly influencing flavor quality.
Citrus juices contain limonin and naringin as the primary bitter components, and their levels serve as a key indicator for juice quality assessment.

Cara Cara navel orange exhibits differential regulation of chalcone synthase (CHS) and chalcone isomerase (CHI) genes during fruit maturation, which modulates the accumulation of flavonoids such as hesperidin.
Thomson navel orange (Citrus × aurantium var. sinensis L.) peel polar extract is primarily composed of flavanone glycosides, including hesperidin and narirutin.
Mandarin orange (Citrus reticulata Blanco) and its hybrids contain hesperidin, eriocitrin, and nobiletin, though their concentrations vary significantly across cultivars.

Navel orange (Citrus sinensis Osbeck) tissues show distinct flavonoid distribution: the flavedo is dominated by polymethoxyflavones (PMFs), while the albedo, segment membrane, and juice sac primarily contain hesperidin and naringin.

Citrus reticulata Blanco and its hybrids exhibit significant cultivar-specific variation in the composition and content of polymethoxyflavones, including nobiletin and tangeretin, according to metabolomic studies.
Zhishi (Citrus aurantium fruit) contains the alkaloid synephrine as a characteristic component of its medicinal profile, and synephrine distribution within the fruit shows clear tissue specificity.
Naringenin, a citrus flavonoid, forms stable mono- and bis-adducts with methylglyoxal (MG), as confirmed by NMR spectroscopy, which may underlie its anti-glycation activity.
Triterpenoid compounds from sour orange (Citrus aurantium L.) inhibit the proliferation of human colon cancer HT-29 cells in vitro by specifically inducing G2/M phase cell cycle arrest.

Citrus medica L. yields the furanocoumarin derivative bergamottin, which pharmacological studies suggest may modulate lipid metabolism homeostasis in liver cancer cells via the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway.

Nanfeng Miju (Citrus reticulata 'Nanfeng') features a thin, smooth rind and translucent juice sacs, with sucrose and fructose as dominant sugars and trace malic acid contributing to a classic profile of pure sweetness with mild acidity.

Navel Orange (Citrus sinensis 'Navel') exhibits a navel-like formation at the fruit apex and is seedless, which promotes concentrated sugar accumulation; its pulp achieves a soluble solids content of 12%–15% and low acidity (pH ≈ 3.5), yielding a purely sweet and refreshing taste.

Lemon (Citrus limon), a hybrid of citron and sour orange, contains high citric acid (4–6 g/100 mL) and trace naringin, resulting in sharp acidity with a subtly bitter finish, and is widely used for flavoring and beverages.
Arginine in mature Shitougan (Citrus species) sac tissue has a taste activity value (TAV) of 4.13 and is a key contributor to the fruit’s bitter taste.
Naringin in mature Shitougan (Citrus species) sac tissue has a TAV of 2.15 and imparts a characteristic lingering bitterness to the fruit.
Mandarin orange (Citrus reticulata Blanco) peel shows cultivar-dependent nobiletin content.
Cold-pressed sweet orange (Citrus sinensis) essential oil contains β-myrcene as a key terpene.
β-Myrcene has a low odor threshold and is a major contributor to the typical fruity citrus flavor.
Yongquan Miju (Citrus reticulata 'Yongquan'), a specialty of Yongquan Town, Linhai City, Zhejiang Province, is renowned for its “eat-with-the-peel” consumption method.
Yongquan Miju (Citrus reticulata 'Yongquan') peel is low in oil glands and has minimal bitterness.
Meishan Chunjian (Citrus reticulata 'Chunjian'), commonly known as Papagan, is a specialty winter orange of Meishan City, Sichuan Province.
Meishan Chunjian (Citrus reticulata 'Chunjian') has orange-colored, crisp, tender, juicy flesh with high sugar, rich flavor, and few or no seeds.
Meishan Chunjian (Citrus reticulata 'Chunjian') achieves 14%–16% soluble solids and 0.5–0.7 g/100 mL citric acid under ecological cultivation.
Meishan Chunjian (Citrus reticulata 'Chunjian') delivers a balanced sweet-sour flavor and crisp-melting texture, earning it the title “Taste Miracle at 30°N Latitude.”
Yongchun Ponkan (Citrus reticulata 'Yongchun'), produced in Yongchun County, Fujian Province, is acclaimed as the “Fine Fruit of the East.”
Yongchun Ponkan (Citrus reticulata 'Yongchun') is prized in domestic and international markets for its large size, bright color, crisp-tender flesh, abundant juice, and melting texture.
Pujiang Shiranui (Citrus reticulata 'Shiranui'), a China National Geographical Indication product from Pujiang County, Chengdu, Sichuan, has an orange-yellow, somewhat coarse rind.
Pujiang Shiranui (Citrus reticulata 'Shiranui') features crisp, tender, juicy flesh with a refreshing sweet-sour taste.
Jiaogan (Citrus reticulata 'Jiao'), native to Guangdong, has rind color ranging from orange-yellow to deep orange-yellow.
Jiaogan (Citrus reticulata 'Jiao') flesh is bright red, soft, very juicy, and clear-sweet, with a long shelf life.
Jiaogan (Citrus reticulata 'Jiao') is cultivated in Guangdong, Guangxi, Fujian, Sichuan, Taiwan, and other regions.
Yichang Miju (Citrus reticulata 'Yichang'), produced in Yichang, Hubei Province—the “Hometown of Chinese Miju”—bears oblate fruit.
Yichang Miju (Citrus reticulata 'Yichang') has a thin, smooth rind and fine-textured, tender flesh with a pleasant sweet-sour flavor.

Shatian Pomelo (Citrus grandis 'Shatian') has crisp flesh rich in naringin and neohesperidin, with low total sugar but a high fructose proportion that creates a distinctive balance of slight bitterness and clear sweetness, which slightly diminishes after storage.

Bitter oranges (e.g., Manao Gan, Ou Gan) have rough rinds and juice sac walls rich in limonoids; after storage, their bitterness decreases while sugar increases, yielding an initial-bitter-to-sweet flavor profile common north of the Wuling Mountains.

Ehime No. 38 (Citrus unshiu × Citrus reticulata 'Ehime No. 38') has an extremely thin segment membrane due to low lignin and cellulose content, resulting in soft, easily fragmentable pulp, low shear and puncture forces, and a “dissolving-in-the-mouth” texture with almost no residue.
Valencia orange (Citrus sinensis) has high lignin content in the pulp, which imparts a coarse, fibrous texture during chewing, making it primarily suitable for juicing rather than fresh consumption.
Satsuma mandarin (Citrus unshiu) has low protopectin content in its segment membrane, achieving high mastication scores with minimal chewing residue.
Gonggan (Citrus reticulata 'Gonggan') pulp features high soluble solids (12%–15%) and moderate citric acid (0.3–0.4 g/100 mL), delivering rich sweetness and a refreshing, melting texture.

Hongmeiren (Citrus unshiu × Citrus reticulata 'Ehime No. 28') achieves a sugar-acid ratio as high as 27.6, with a segment membrane less than half the thickness of ordinary citrus, resulting in no perceptible fibrous sensation and superior mastication.
Shatangju (Citrus reticulata 'Shatangju') has a sugar-acid ratio >12.0, with sucrose accounting for 57% of total sugars, yielding dominant sweetness complemented by malic acid–derived crispness.

Zhongshan Gonggan (Citrus reticulata 'Zhongshan Gonggan') accumulates carotenoids in the peel during December–January maturation and develops crisp, melting flesh with a honey-like, non-cloying sweetness.

Chaozhou Gan (Citrus reticulata 'Chaozhou') has a thick, orange-yellow rind with dense oil glands and high levels of limonene and other volatile terpenes that impart a strong floral aroma; its pulp offers a balanced sugar-acid ratio, clear sweetness, and subtle astringency.

Grapefruit (Citrus × paradisi) flesh is rich in naringin, has low total sugar but a high fructose proportion, and exhibits strong bitterness and acidity—citric acid comprising 66%–99%—creating a sharp sensory contrast that underpins its common use in weight-loss diets.

Bergamot (Citrus medica var. sarcodactylis) has a thick rind rich in volatile oils; the synergy between linalool and limonene produces a woody-floral aroma with a spicy-sweet aftertaste, while its sour and astringent pulp is primarily used for flavoring and medicinal purposes.

In Shaitian citrus, the contents of organic acids such as quinic acid and aconitic acid in juice sacs decline during fruit development and fall below their sourness perception thresholds at maturity, resulting in minimal contribution to overall sourness.
Limonin is a key contributor to lingering bitterness in citrus juices.

Naringin, a flavanone glycoside with a rhamnosyl group at the C-2 position of its glucoside, imparts intense, persistent bitterness; its concentration in Shaitian citrus segment membrane declines from 6.17 mg/g (immature) to 3.45 mg/g (mature).

Neohesperidin, like naringin, is a major flavonoid bitter compound in citrus; in Shaitian citrus, it is highly enriched in the segment membrane over juice sacs, and its mature content (3.45 mg/g) remains above the bitterness threshold, directly driving membrane bitterness.

Citric acid dominates sourness in citrus juice sacs, accounting for 70–90% of total organic acids, with a rapid but short-lived sour sensation; in Shaitian citrus, its content drops sharply from 21.17 mg/g to 4.73 mg/g during maturation, markedly reducing sourness intensity.

Sucrose and fructose in mature Shaitian citrus juice sacs both exceed taste thresholds and together constitute over 57.6% of soluble sugars (with glucose), serving as the main drivers of sweetness, with distinct accumulation patterns between juice sacs and segment membrane.

Arginine, a bitter amino acid, exhibits a high taste activity value (TAV = 8.26) in mature Shaitian citrus juice sacs—well above the TAV ≥1 threshold—and, together with flavonoids and limonoids, forms a complex bitter background.

Nomilin, the second most abundant limonoid after limonin, decreases in Shaitian citrus segment membrane from 0.60 mg/g (young fruit) to 0.002 mg/g (maturity), yet remains a non-negligible bitterness source in some varieties.

Sweet: Pleasing and easy on the palate, it can go from gentle and nice, to delightful and attractive, tends to be satisfying, enjoyable and rewarding, may or may not be sugary.
SUGARY: The smell of the sweetness of sugar, this can be a cooked or an uncooked smell, it belongs to Sweet.
SCENTED: The scent of perfume can have a background or a forefront smell, it belongs to Sweet.
FRAGRANT: Very forward on the nose, can have a lot of aspects at one time, it belongs to Sweet.
AMBROSIAL: Divine, sweet-smelling, fragrant, aromatic, it belongs to Sweet.
NUTTY: A toasted type of aroma that smells usually of a cooked product and warmth, it belongs to Sweet.
CARAMELIZED: The smell of cooked sugar very rich in smell can also have an earthly tone, it belongs to Sweet.
CHOCOLATEY: Smells rich and deep in scent, it belongs to Sweet.
Spicy: A scent that is very powerful, allowing you can smell the heat and spiciness, can be very fulfilling to overwhelming, often very strong.
PIQUANT: Stinging, an aroma that tickles the nose. This is a feeling as well as an aroma, it belongs to Spicy.
HEADY: This is a very strong smell that is also rich, intoxicating,spiced, very filling, it belongs to Spicy.
PUNGENT: This is a strong aroma. It is spicy, hot, overpowering,maybe sharp or bitter. It is a very distinct smell and very forward, it belongs to Spicy.
WARMING: When a scent fills the nose and warms the senses starting to impact the taste, it belongs to Spicy.
SPICED: The essence of ingredients standing out. Things like cinnamon, clove,anise,nutmeg, it belongs to Spicy.
PEPPERY: The aroma of pepper as a spice, very strong on the nose and pronounced, it belongs to Spicy.
FIERY: The scent that most closely goes with the flavor of heat, it belongs to Spicy.
Savory: A savory aroma the smell can be flavorsome, full smelling, salty and not sweet. Often pleasant, enjoyable, and wholesome.
GAMEY: Having the distinctive fragrance of game meats. This is a semistrong but even scent, things like lamb and venison have a gamey scent, it belongs to Savory.
FULSOME: Generous to excess. A very full smell, often hearty, it belongs to Savory.
Comforting: A pleasant aroma, having a feeling and scent of home.A calming smell, it belongs to Savory.
BUTTERY: A very smooth aroma, often associated with baked goods, it belongs to Savory.
Full-bodied: Fills the whole nose with fragrance, it belongs to Savory.
APPETIZING: Something that produces an attractive smell, it belongs to Savory.
BAKED: The smell of warmth. Can have hints of sugary, buttery, and comforting, it belongs to Savory.
BRINY: The smell of natural salt in a dish or in an ingredient, it belongs to Savory.
Earthy: The natural smells of the earth can come from things like the soil, the climate, and the freshness of the products.
FRESH: The aroma is clean, clear, cool, refreshing, sweet and new,crisp as newly picked herbs or vegetables, it belongs to Earthy.
FLORAL: The smell of flowers, can be found in herbs and some fruits, it belongs to Earthy.
AGED: The natural smell of a product as it deepens and has a fuller body of flavor. Can have an almost musty smell, but not overwhelmingly so, it belongs to Earthy.
SMOKEY: The smell from cold or hot smoking. Heavily caramelized vegetables can begin to smell smokey, even without the addition of smoke, it belongs to Earthy.
HERBAL: The smell of herbs and fresh greens. A natural and fresh smell, it belongs to Earthy.
Earthiness: The natural smell of the earth, can have organic scents of soil and forest, it belongs to Earthy.
WOODY: The smell or aroma of wood. Often this is more of a background flavor from cooking or added ingredients, it belongs to Earthy.
Fruity: The smell of fruits and fruitiness in food. Usually, a perky smell which stands out and many times has some scents of earthy, sugar and freshness.
FRESH FRUIT: The smell of all fruits at the peak of their season. Very filling scents with hints of sugar and sometimes herbal.Think fresh berries, it belongs to Fruity.
CITRUSY: The scents of citrus fruit, often have a small amount of tart or tanginess. Citrus fruits are very forward and fruity, it belongs to Fruity.
TROPICAL FRUIT: The smell of the fruits from warm climates. A lot of natural sugars and a lot of times a very smooth and buttery scent.Think pineapple and mango, it belongs to Fruity.

BLACK FRUIT: The smell of fruits from a cooler climate. Can have a scent of tartness as well as sugar. Usually, very deep flavored fruits that are deep in color. Think cherries and plums, it belongs to Fruity.
TREE FRUIT: Fruit scents that have a very natural scent. They have background scents of earthiness and small amounts of herbs. Think pears and apples, it belongs to Fruity.

Chewiness：How well bits of a food slides past another without breaking.
CHEWY: The texture of a food that needs to be chewed thoroughly before swallowing. Can be light and bouncy or heavy and sticky, it belongs to Chewiness.
DOUGHY: A soft and heavy texture that is often coupled with pale coloring. Like a thick deep-dish pizza, it belongs to Chewiness.
GOOEY: A viscous, sometimes sticky texture arising from the presence of moisture in a dense solid food, it belongs to Chewiness.
STICKY: A texture characterized by gluiness in the mouth. This can be like honey or maple syrup, or that warm glaze on the outside of ribs and bbq food, it belongs to Chewiness.
Graininess: The size of particles in a food product.
SILKY: A fine, smooth texture characterized by a sleek feel in the mouth. A butternut squash soup or lobster bisque would be great examples, it belongs to Graininess.
SMOOTH: A consistent texture free of grit, lumps, or indentations. Like a sauce of veloute that would go onto a protein or a handmade mayonnaise, it belongs to Graininess.
VELVETY: An extremely smooth and oftentimes fatty texture. Often used to describe decadent desserts. Can also be used to describe a heavy cream-based dish, it belongs to Graininess.
GRAINY: Things are gritty, textured with little bumps or grains. The grain can be clearly discerned in the product. Polenta or grits will feel grainy, it belongs to Graininess.
Brittleness: How easily food shatters or breaks apart.
CRISPY: A light texture with a slight crunch. Like freshly cooked fried chicken, it belongs to Brittleness.
CRUMBLY: The texture of a food with a loose structure that falls apart into small pieces or crumbs. Breakfast breads are a great example, it belongs to Brittleness.
CRUNCHY: A firm, crisp texture often identified by the sharp, audible noise that the food makes when being eaten. Like kettle-cooked chips, or pork rinds, it belongs to Brittleness.
DELICATE: A light, fine texture that may come apart easily. This can be like a ladyfinger on the outside of a tiramisu, it belongs to Brittleness.
FLAKY: A light texture characterized by layers that come apart during eating. A great croissant is flaky in texture, it belongs to Brittleness.
Firmness: Resistance to pressure.
AIRY: A light and pillowy texture often created by the incorporation of air. Think of a souffle from the addition of whipped egg whites, it belongs to Firmness.
FLUFFY: A light and airy texture. Angel food cake is often described as fluffy, it belongs to Firmness.
JUICY: A succulent, tender texture characterized by the presence of liquid in a solid food. Like biting into the fresh peach or strawberry in the summer, it belongs to Firmness.
SUCCULENT: A tender, juicy texture with the presence of sweetness. Often described in dessert-like. A devil's food cake or a chocolate lava cake, it belongs to Firmness.
TENDER: A soft texture that is easy to break down. Think of beef tenderloin, short ribs, braised chicken legs, it belongs to Firmness.
Consistency: Thinness or thickness of a product.
BUTTERY: A smooth and creamy texture similar to that of butter. Think about a fresh biscuit or a fresh-baked croissant, it belongs to Consistency.

CREAMY: A smooth and rich texture that usually comes from the incorporation of dairy. This can also be the techniques applied such as the starch from making a risotto or mashing a potato, it belongs to Consistency.

Citrus unshiu, which is known as Satsuma mandarin, has anti-oxidative, anti-inflammation, and anti-microviral activity.
We found that extract of premature C. unshiu reduced DNCB-induced symptoms such as hyperkeratosis, increased skin thickness, and infiltrated mast cells, in our AD-like animal model.
Also, extract of premature C. unshiu inhibited mRNA expression and protein production of TARC and MDC through the inhibition of STAT1 phosphorylation.

Citrus unshiu is a kind of citrus fruit in the Rutaceae family. C. unshiu is composed of rind and sarcocarp and includes various bioactive substances such as essential oils, carotenoids, cellulose, pectin, limonoid, etc.
In recent studies, it has been reported that flavonoids are also contained in C. unshiu extracts which have anti-oxidant, anti-cancer, and anti-inflammatory activity.

Premature C. unshiu contains flavonoids such as naringin, hesperidin, neohesperidin, narirutin, nobiletin, etc., that are known to have anti-inflammation, anti-oxidant, anti-diabetes, and antiallergy effects in vitro and in vivo.
